concepts.def: Distance is how far an object moves along the path it actually travels. It does not involve direction, so it is a scalar quantity: a magnitude and a unit fully describe it, for example 450 m.

Displacement is the distance an object moves measured in a straight line from the start point to the finish point, together with the direction of that straight line. It is quoted as a magnitude and a direction, for example 450 m due east.
A scalar quantity has magnitude only. Distance and speed are scalars: stating the number and the unit says everything there is to say about them.
A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction. Displacement and velocity are vectors: two vectors of the same size pointing different ways are different quantities.
Speed is how fast an object is moving. It does not involve direction, so speed is a scalar quantity, measured in metres per second, m/s.
The specification gives typical values that may be taken as: walking about 1.5 m/s, running about 3 m/s and cycling about 6 m/s. These are estimates to be recalled and used, not exact figures.

Students should also be able to recall typical speeds for different types of transportation system, for example a car on a motorway at roughly 30 m/s, a train at roughly 50 m/s and an aeroplane at roughly 250 m/s.
The speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle depends on many factors including age, terrain, fitness and the distance travelled.

The speed of a moving object is rarely constant: when people walk, run or travel in a car their speed changes constantly. It is not only moving objects that have varying speed, because the speed of sound and the speed of the wind also vary.
A typical value for the speed of sound in air is 330 m/s. The actual value varies, for example with the temperature of the air.
Speed is found by measuring a distance, for example with a ruler, tape measure or trundle wheel, measuring the time taken with a stopwatch or light gates, and then dividing the distance by the time.
For an object moving at constant speed the distance travelled in a specific time can be calculated using distance travelled = speed × time, written in symbols as [s = v t].

concepts.term: Quantities and units in [s = v t]
concepts.def: In s = v t the distance s is in metres, m; the speed v is in metres per second, m/s; and the time t is in seconds, s.
For non-uniform motion the average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken, including any time spent stationary.
The velocity of an object is its speed in a given direction, so velocity is a vector quantity. Two objects with equal speeds have different velocities if they move in different directions.
Distance and speed are scalars; displacement and velocity are the matching vector quantities. Each pair has the same unit, and the vector member of the pair also carries a direction.

An object moving in a circle at a steady rate has constant speed but changing velocity, because its direction of motion changes continuously. Examples include a car on a roundabout and a satellite in a circular orbit.
If an object moves along a straight line, the distance travelled can be represented by a distance-time graph, with time on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis.

The speed of an object can be calculated from the gradient of its distance-time graph: gradient is the change in distance divided by the change in time. A horizontal line has zero gradient, so the object is stationary.

concepts.term: Tangent to a distance-time graph (HT only)
concepts.def: If an object is accelerating, its speed at any particular time can be determined by drawing a tangent to the curve at that time and measuring the gradient of that tangent.
Students should be able to draw distance-time graphs from measurements, and extract and interpret lines and slopes, translating information between graphical and numerical form.
The average acceleration of an object can be calculated using acceleration = (change in velocity)/(time taken), written in symbols as [a = (∆v)/(t)].
Acceleration, a, is in metres per second squared, m/s^2; change in velocity, ∆ v, is in metres per second, m/s; and time, t, is in seconds, s.
An object that slows down is decelerating. Its acceleration has the opposite sign to its velocity, so for an object moving forwards the acceleration is negative.
Students should be able to estimate the magnitude of everyday accelerations, for example a family car pulling away at roughly 2 m/s^2 and an object falling freely at about 9.8 m/s^2.

The acceleration of an object can be calculated from the gradient of a velocity-time graph. Students should be able to draw velocity-time graphs from measurements and interpret lines and slopes to determine acceleration.

concepts.term: Area under a velocity-time graph (HT only)
concepts.def: The distance travelled by an object, or the displacement of an object, can be calculated from the area under a velocity-time graph, and students should be able to interpret enclosed areas to determine it.
Where the area under a velocity-time graph is not a simple triangle or rectangle, it can be measured, when appropriate, by counting squares and multiplying by the quantity one square represents.
The following equation applies to uniform acceleration: (final velocity)^2 - (initial velocity)^2 = 2 × acceleration × distance, written in symbols as [v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s].

concepts.term: Quantities and units in [v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s]
concepts.def: Final velocity v and initial velocity u are in metres per second, m/s; acceleration a is in metres per second squared, m/s^2; and distance s is in metres, m.
Near the Earth's surface any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s^2, whatever its mass.

An object falling through a fluid initially accelerates due to the force of gravity. As it speeds up the drag force grows until eventually the resultant force is zero and the object moves at its terminal velocity. Physics only: students should be able to draw and interpret velocity-time graphs for objects that reach terminal velocity and interpret the changing motion in terms of the forces acting.

mcqs.q: A student walks 30 m due east along a corridor and then walks 30 m back to the point where she started. What are the distance she has travelled and her displacement?
options: Distance 60 m; displacement zero, as she ends where she began
Distance 60 m; displacement 60 m, as both measure her walk
Distance 60 m; displacement 30 m, the furthest point reached
Distance 30 m; displacement 30 m west, using the return leg
mcqs.explain: Distance is measured along the whole path walked, 30 m + 30 m = 60 m. The straight line from start point to finish point has no length, so the displacement is zero.

mcqs.q: A walker sets off from a car park, goes 3.0 km due east and then 4.0 km due north. Which of these correctly expresses her displacement from the car park?
options: 7.0 km, on a heading 37 degrees east of north
5.0 km, in a direction 37 degrees east of north
5.0 km, and no direction needs to be stated
1.0 km, due north of the car park she left
mcqs.explain: The two legs are at right angles, so the magnitude is the square root of (3.0^2 + 4.0^2) = 5.0 km, and a displacement must also carry the direction of that straight line.

mcqs.q: Which pair contains only scalar quantities?
options: Speed and velocity, as both describe how fast it goes
Distance and displacement, as both are lengths in metres
Distance and speed, as neither has a direction
Displacement and velocity, both having a size
mcqs.explain: Distance is how far an object moves and speed is how fast it moves; neither involves direction, so both are scalars.

mcqs.q: Which quantity is only fully described when a direction is given as well as a number and a unit?
options: Distance, measured along the path
The time taken, measured in seconds
Speed, measured in metres per second
Displacement, a vector quantity
mcqs.explain: Displacement is a vector: it is the straight-line distance from start to finish together with the direction of that line, so both parts must be stated.

mcqs.q: Two cars travel along the same straight road at 20 m/s, one heading north and the other heading south. Which statement is correct?
options: Their speeds are equal but their velocities differ
Their speeds and their velocities are both equal
Their speeds differ, but their velocities match
Neither their speeds nor velocities are equal
mcqs.explain: Speed is a scalar, so both are 20 m/s. Velocity is speed in a given direction, and the directions are opposite, so the velocities differ.

mcqs.q: Why is the speed of a car driven across a busy town rarely constant?
options: Cars are built to hold a single steady speed once moving
The driver keeps changing speed at junctions and bends
Speed can only change when the direction changes too
A speedometer shows the average speed of the trip
mcqs.explain: The speed of a moving object is rarely constant: when people walk, run or travel in a car their speed is constantly changing.

mcqs.q: Which list gives factors that affect the speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle?
options: Fitness alone, as everybody else walks at 1.5 m/s
Terrain and distance only, as age has no effect on it
Age, fitness, terrain and the distance travelled
Only terrain, since a person's speed is fixed
mcqs.explain: The specification lists age, terrain, fitness and distance travelled among the many factors affecting the speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle.

mcqs.q: Which is the best estimate of the typical speed of a person walking?
options: 6.0 m/s, close to 22 km/h
15 m/s, or roughly 54 km/h
0.15 m/s, or about 0.5 km/h
1.5 m/s, or about 5 km/h
mcqs.explain: The specification gives walking as about 1.5 m/s, which is roughly 5 km/h - a familiar walking pace.

mcqs.q: A student is asked to use typical values for the speeds of a runner and a cyclist. Which pair should she use?
options: Running about 3 m/s and cycling about 6 m/s
Running about 6 m/s, cycling about 3 m/s
Running near 3 m/s, cycling near 3 m/s
Running 1.5 m/s, cycling about 6 m/s
mcqs.explain: The specification gives running as about 3 m/s and cycling as about 6 m/s, roughly double the running value.

mcqs.q: Which is the most sensible typical speed to quote for a car travelling along a motorway?
options: About 300 m/s, which is close to the speed of sound
About 30 m/s, which is roughly 70 miles per hour
About 10 m/s, a little faster than a cyclist
About 3 m/s, about a person's running pace
mcqs.explain: A motorway speed of about 30 m/s is close to 70 mph and is the usual typical value quoted for a car.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the speed of sound in air is correct?
options: It is fixed at 300 000 000 m/s in every case
It is always exactly 330 m/s, whatever the air
It varies, but a typical value is 330 m/s
It varies, but a typical value is 33 m/s
mcqs.explain: The specification gives a typical value of 330 m/s and notes that the speed of sound, like the speed of the wind, varies.

mcqs.q: A student sees a flash of lightning and hears the thunder 6.0 s later. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m/s, how far away was the lightning?
mcqs.explain: Using distance travelled = speed × time, s = v t = 330 m/s × 6.0 s = 1980 m.

mcqs.q: A train travels at a constant speed of 45 m/s. How long does it take to travel 9.0 km?
mcqs.explain: Rearranging s = v t gives t = s / v. Converting 9.0 km to 9000 m, t = 9000 / 45 = 200 s.

mcqs.q: A student wants to measure the average speed of a trolley rolling down a ramp. Which method should she use?
options: Measure the distance travelled and the time taken, then multiply these
Measure the distance travelled and the time taken, then divide distance by time
Measure the distance and the time, then divide the time by the distance
Measure the time for the trip twice and then find the mean of them
mcqs.explain: Speed is found by making measurements of distance and of time and then dividing the distance by the time taken.

mcqs.q: A car's speed changes constantly during a journey through town. How should its average speed for the journey be found?
options: Add together the highest and the lowest speeds, then halve that
Divide the total time taken by the total distance moved
Divide the total distance travelled by the total time taken
Read the speedometer at the halfway point of the trip
mcqs.explain: Average speed for non-uniform motion is the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken, including any time spent stopped.

mcqs.q: A cyclist rides 4.0 km in 500 s, rests for 100 s, and then rides 5.0 km in 400 s. What is her average speed for the whole journey?
options: 10 m/s
8 m/s
mcqs.explain: Total distance is 9000 m and total time is 1000 s, so the average speed is 9000 / 1000 = 9.0 m/s.

mcqs.q: Which statement best describes the velocity of a moving object?
options: Speed in a given direction
Simply another word for speed
How far it travels each second
How quickly its direction changes
mcqs.explain: The velocity of an object is its speed in a given direction, which makes velocity a vector quantity.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly classifies distance, displacement, speed and velocity?
options: Distance and displacement are scalars, with the others vectors
Distance and speed are scalars; displacement and velocity are vectors
Distance and velocity are scalars, displacement and speed vectors
All four are vectors, since each one has a size and a unit
mcqs.explain: Distance and speed carry no direction, so they are scalars; displacement and velocity each include a direction, so they are vectors.

mcqs.q: A car is driven round a roundabout at a steady 8 m/s. Which statement about its motion is correct?
options: Both its speed and its velocity stay constant all round
Its velocity is constant but its speed is changing
Its speed is constant but its velocity keeps changing
Neither its speed nor its velocity is constant
mcqs.explain: Motion in a circle involves constant speed but changing velocity, because the direction of motion changes continuously.

mcqs.q: What does the gradient of a distance-time graph tell you about the object?
options: The acceleration at that time
The distance moved so far
The total time of the trip
The speed at that moment
mcqs.explain: The speed of an object can be calculated from the gradient of its distance-time graph: change in distance divided by change in time.

mcqs.q: On a distance-time graph a straight line passes through the origin and through the point (8.0 s, 120 m). What is the speed of the object?
options: 15 m/s
8 m/s
mcqs.explain: The gradient is the change in distance divided by the change in time: 120 m / 8.0 s = 15 m/s.

mcqs.q: Part of a distance-time graph for a car is a horizontal straight line. What is the car doing during that part?
options: It is moving at a steady speed there
It is stationary and staying put
It is going back towards the start
It is speeding up all the time
mcqs.explain: A horizontal line has zero gradient, so the distance is not changing and the speed is zero.

mcqs.q: The distance-time graph for an accelerating car is a curve. How should the speed of the car at 6 s be found?
options: Join the origin to the point at 6 s and find that gradient
Read the distance at 6 s straight off the vertical axis
Draw a tangent to the curve at 6 s and measure its gradient
Find the area under the curve up to the 6 s point
mcqs.explain: For an accelerating object the speed at a particular time is the gradient of the tangent drawn to the distance-time graph at that time.

mcqs.q: On a distance-time graph the line curves upwards and becomes steeper as time goes on. What does this show?
options: The object is slowing down as time goes on
The object moves at a steady high speed
The object is moving away from the start
The object is speeding up as time goes on
mcqs.explain: An increasing gradient means the distance covered each second is growing, so the object is speeding up.

mcqs.q: A motorbike speeds up from 5 m/s to 29 m/s in 6.0 s. What is its average acceleration?
options: 24 m/s
mcqs.explain: Using a = (change in velocity) / t, the change in velocity is 29 - 5 = 24 m/s, so a = 24 / 6.0 = 4 m/s^2.

mcqs.q: A train slows down uniformly from 30 m/s to 10 m/s in 40 s. Which statement is correct?
options: It is now travelling backwards along the track at 10 m/s
It is decelerating, and so its acceleration is -0.5 m/s^2
It is decelerating at 0.25 m/s^2, from 10 m/s in 40 s
It is accelerating at 0.5 m/s^2 along the track
mcqs.explain: An object that slows down is decelerating. The change in velocity is -20 m/s in 40 s, so the acceleration is -0.5 m/s^2.

mcqs.q: Which is the best estimate of the acceleration of a family car pulling away from traffic lights?
options: About 100 m/s^2, so reaching 12 m/s in around 0.1 s
About 9.8 m/s^2, the same as an object falling
About 2 m/s^2, reaching some 12 m/s in about 6 s
About 0.02 m/s^2, reaching 12 m/s in 10 min
mcqs.explain: A sensible everyday estimate: 2 m/s^2 sustained for 6 s gives 12 m/s, a reasonable town speed.

mcqs.q: What does the gradient of a velocity-time graph give?
options: The distance it has travelled
The speed it has at that moment
The average velocity so far
The object's acceleration
mcqs.explain: The acceleration of an object can be calculated from the gradient of a velocity-time graph.

mcqs.q: A velocity-time graph for a cyclist is a straight line rising from 0 m/s to 15 m/s over 8.0 s. What distance does the cyclist travel in that time?
mcqs.explain: The distance is the area under the line, a triangle: 0.5 × 8.0 s × 15 m/s = 60 m.

mcqs.q: A car accelerates uniformly at 3.5 m/s^2 from an initial velocity of 24 m/s over a distance of 7.0 m. What is its final velocity?
options: 25 m/s
7 m/s

mcqs.q: A ball is dropped near the Earth's surface. Ignoring air resistance, what is its acceleration as it falls?
options: About 9.8 m/s^2 if the ball is heavy
About 9.8 m/s, growing as the ball falls
About 9.8 m/s^2, directed downwards
Zero, as it falls at steady speed
mcqs.explain: Near the Earth's surface any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s^2.

mcqs.q: A skydiver falling through the air reaches terminal velocity. Which statement describes what is happening?
options: Gravity has stopped acting, so no force acts at all now
The skydiver slows down and stops falling in the air
The air resistance is now larger than the skydiver's weight
The resultant force is zero, so velocity is steady
mcqs.explain: The drag force grows as the skydiver speeds up until it balances the weight; with zero resultant force the velocity stays constant.

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.5.6.1 Forces and motion: Describing motion along a line
